title: Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar 5140G in 18k White Gold Opaline dial with Box and Extract of Archives
description: We have always been big fans of perpetual calendars, and few brands are as closely associated with the complication as Patek Philippe. Not only did the manufacture play a pivotal role in the development of the perpetual calendar wristwatch, it also helped establish the market for complicated wristwatches as we know it today. Presented here is a lovely reference 5140G in 18k white gold, featuring an elegant and perfectly proportioned 37 mm case. The reference 5140 succeeded the legendary 3940, a model widely regarded as one of the most important creations of Patek Philippe's modern era. Together with the reference 3970, the 3940 helped redefine complicated watchmaking in the late twentieth century and is often considered one of the first highly complicated wristwatches to be produced in series. After an impressive production run spanning nearly two decades, the 3940 was replaced in 2006 by the reference 5140, which retained the celebrated ultra-thin self-winding calibre 240Q, powered by a beautifully engineered micro-rotor. The elegant white-gold case features the four correctors required to adjust the perpetual calendar functions and remains in excellent condition, with the gold hallmarks still clearly visible. The watch is fitted with its beautiful snap-on sapphire display case back, offering a wonderful view of the exquisite calibre 240Q movement. Our watchmaker has fully checked and regulated the movement to ensure it performs exactly as it should. The opaline dial is both refined and highly legible, featuring a dotted minute track and three perfectly balanced sub-dials displaying the perpetual calendar indications. These include the date, day, month, leap-year cycle, 24-hour indication, and moon-phase display, all presented in English. The dial's clean layout and understated elegance are hallmarks of what many collectors consider one of Patek Philippe's finest perpetual calendar designs. Completing the watch is its original Patek Philippe leather strap, fitted with an 18k white-gold Patek Philippe folding clasp.Further more the original 18 k white gold second closed case back is also included in the sale as well the original wooden Patek Philippe box with its battery driven watch winder. Accompanied by a Patek Philippe Extract from the Archives confirming that the watch was originally sold in 2014. For collectors looking to enter the world of Patek Philippe “Grand Complications,” this piece represents an exceptional opportunity. It combines elegant proportions, everyday wearability, and the timeless appeal of one of the brand’s most respected modern perpetual calendar designs. Understated yet highly sophisticated, it remains an enduring classic within the Patek Philippe collection.For further details or to discuss availability, feel free to get in touch. title: Rolex GMT-Master 1675 MK1 Long-E unique Tropical Dial

However, tropical-dial versions—where the original black dial has naturally aged to a rich brown hue—remain particularly rare and highly sought after. These dials are found only within a specific serial range and exclusively on the coveted Mark 1 (“MK1”) dial, distinguished by the elongated center stroke of the “E” in Rolex, commonly referred to as the “Long E.” Encountering a genuine tropical “Long E” is always a special occasion. The transformation of the dial into a warm milk-chocolate brown gives the watch remarkable character and depth, while the luminous material on the hands and hour markers has aged gracefully to a soft beige tone, creating a beautiful and harmonious patina. The watch is further enhanced by a well-preserved red-back Pepsi bezel insert. Over time, the colors have matured beautifully: the red has softened to a vibrant orange, while the blue has evolved into a striking Mediterranean-sea blue, producing a wonderfully balanced and highly attractive appearance. With its rare tropical dial, beautifully aged bezel, and unmistakable vintage charm, this “Long E” GMT-Master 1675 is a truly captivating collector’s piece—an opportunity seldom encountered and not to be missed ! Affectionately known as the "President," the Day-Date has adorned the wrists of heads of state, business leaders, and discerning collectors for decades and remains exclusively crafted in precious metals. As we often say, it whispers rather than shouts. The silver soleil-finished dial pairs perfectly with the white-gold case and features crisp black printing, applied baton hour markers, and beautifully aged cream-coloured luminous accents. Powered by Rolex's reliable automatic movement, that has been fully serviced by our watch maker.This Day-Date offers everything collectors admire about the model: timeless design, precious-metal construction, and an understated elegance that has made it a symbol of success for 70 years ! A discreet and highly wearable Day-Date, ready for its next custodian. Contact us to learn more. While the original 1953 Explorer was built for mountain climbing, the Explorer II was engineered with a fixed 24-hour bezel and a prominent 24-hour arrow hand to help users distinguish between AM and PM when cut off from natural sunlight. With the introduction of the second generation, Rolex introduced white dials on the reference 16550 in 1985. In 1989, Rolex upgraded the model with the new caliber 3185/3186 in the reference 16570 — and that is exactly what we have to offer here. The Polar white dial is in superb condition, with black printed text, black-outlined hour markers, and warm yellow lume on both the plots and hands — always a detail we love to see on these. These so-called "transitional" models bridged the gap between vintage and modern Submariners, combining elements from both generations. Early examples, such as this one, were fitted with matte dials similar to those found on their acrylic-crystal predecessors, many of which were later replaced during service. This excellent example of the Reference 16800 retains its original matte dial, displaying a beautiful soft-yellow patina across the hour markers that perfectly complements the watch's vintage character. title: Vacheron Constantin Coin Watch in 18k Yellow Gold 4928
description: Founded in 1755, Vacheron Constantin is the oldest watch manufacturer in the world to have operated continuously without interruption. Based in Geneva, Switzerland, the Maison has spent more than 270 years crafting exceptional timepieces that blend technical mastery with refined artistic expression. Widely regarded as part of the prestigious “Holy Trinity” of Swiss watchmaking, alongside Patek Philippe and Audemars Piguet, the brand has long stood at the pinnacle of haute horlogerie. Throughout its history, Vacheron Constantin has served royalty, collectors, and connoisseurs alike, earning a reputation for uncompromising craftsmanship, elegant design, and mechanical innovation. Every creation reflects centuries of accumulated expertise, making the manufacture one of the most respected names in Swiss watchmaking. Coin watches are among the most extra ordinary and collectible expressions of horology. These rare creations sit at the intersection of watchmaking, numismatics, and history. Each piece begins as a genuine coin in circulation before being meticulously transformed by a master craftsman. The coin is carefully hollowed out on both sides, a concealed cavity is created to house a miniature movement, and the two halves are then reassembled with a discreet hinged opening system. Among the maisons known for producing such remarkable timepieces is Vacheron Constantin. This exceptional example is crafted from a 1904 twenty-dollar gold coin and is identified by the manufacture as Model 4928. It represents a striking combination of historical significance, technical ingenuity, and refined watchmaking, resulting in a highly collectible and visually captivating work of art. The coin opens via a side-mounted push button, revealing the hidden watch within. Inside, a small champagne-toned dial features painted hour markers and elegant blued stick hands, complemented by a discreet crown positioned at 1 o’clock. The case can also be displayed upright, transforming the piece into a functional desk or table clock—an object designed to be both worn and admired. This example is based on a 1904 twenty-dollar U.S. gold coin with a finely detailed reeded edge and straight lugs. It is fitted with its original Vacheron Constantin strap and a period-correct 18k gold “AW” signed buckle. A Bulang and Sons strap will be supplied with the watch, with the final choice left to the buyer. The hand-wound movement has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready for years of reliable use. We love these Coin watches —they are effortlessly cool, lightweight on the wrist, and an absolute conversation starter! Take a closer look, and let’s have a conversation about this remarkable piece ! title: Patek Philippe World Time 5110J Guilloche Dial in 18k Yellow Gold with Extract of the Archives
description: The story of the Patek Philippe World Time—historically known as Heures Universelles —is deeply intertwined with an era when international travel was still an adventure and crossing continents carried an unmistakable sense of glamour. Conceived during the early 20th century for diplomats, businessmen, and seasoned travellers, the World Time complication enabled its wearer to read all 24 time zones simultaneously at a glance—an extraordinary technical achievement for its day. Over the decades, the World Time evolved from a highly specialised travel instrument into one of the most admired complications in haute horlogerie. Combining mechanical ingenuity with beautifully balanced dial design, it came to represent not only technical sophistication but also a romantic vision of global travel that continues to captivate collectors today. Presented here is the Patek Philippe reference 5110J, with the "J" denoting its elegant 18k yellow gold case. Measuring a perfectly proportioned 37mm, the Calatrava-inspired case is beautifully sculpted, featuring integrated crown guards and Patek Philippe's patented world-time pusher at 10 o'clock. A single press of the pusher simultaneously advances the central hour hand, the 24-hour ring, and the outer city disc in one-hour increments, instantly recalibrating the display across all 24 time zones. It is a wonderfully intuitive and elegant mechanical solution, making one of watchmaking's most complex complications remarkably easy to use. Turning the watch over reveals a sapphire display case back showcasing the exceptional ultra-thin self-winding calibre 240 HU. Equipped with Patek Philippe's beautifully finished 22k gold micro-rotor, the movement is every bit as impressive as the dial it powers. The watch is fitted with a handsome Bulang and Sons leather strap and its original 18k yellow gold Patek Philippe pin buckle. Accompanying the watch is an Extract from the Archives confirming its sale in 2001. The World Time has long been one of our favourite complications at Bulang and Sons, and the 5110J is, in our eyes, one of its most elegant executions. Whether you're crossing continents or simply dreaming about the next destination, this is a watch that inspires travel every time you glance at your wrist. Ready for your next journey? Get in touch. title: Tudor Submariner 7928 MK7 Dial Black-Out Lume
description: The Tudor Submariner is widely regarded as one of the most important and enduring dive watches in horological history, remaining in production from 1954 until its discontinuation in 1999. Created under the vision of Hans Wilsdorf, Tudor was established to deliver the same reliability, robustness, and waterproof performance associated with Rolex, but at a more accessible price point. The Submariner perfectly embodied this philosophy, combining true tool-watch functionality with timeless design and military-grade dependability. At hand we have a late-series reference 7928, presented in very nice overall condition, featuring a strong case and a beautifully faded “fat font” bezel insert. The Tudor Submariner 7928 is closely associated with military use, most notably by U.S. Navy SEALs and Underwater Demolition Teams (UDT) during the Vietnam War era. Documented examples are often linked to so-called “Coronado dials,” with custom modifications carried out in the field or by military watchmakers in Coronado, California, to reduce reflectivity and improve legibility during covert operations. These modifications could include reprinted or hand-painted dials, matte black finishes, and the removal or darkening of luminous material on the indexes and hands. The dial on this example exhibits a similar character, with a darkened, on the original tritium lume appearance on both the markers and hands. It gives the watch a distinctive “dark horse” presence on the wrist—subtle, utilitarian, and full of character. Further enhancing its appeal, the watch features the iconic Tudor rose logo on the Mk7 dial variant. It is fitted to a “Hecho en México” Jubilee bracelet—originally produced for the North and South American markets—which adds an additional layer of period-correct charm and intrigue to this already highly collectible Tudor Submariner. We love finding watches with character, and this one certainly delivers. Get in touch if you'd like to add it to your collection. title: Rolex Millgauss 1019 Silver Dial
description: Before the Rolex Milgauss came along, scientists had a real problem. Magnetic fields as low as 50 to 100 gauss could already throw a mechanical watch completely off. In environments where precision mattered, that simply didn’t cut it—so it was either deal with an unreliable watch or leave it off the wrist altogether. Rolex stepped in with a proper solution. In the 1950s, the Milgauss was tested by CERN—the world’s leading particle physics lab—and proved capable of resisting magnetic fields up to 1,000 gauss. A serious technical achievement at the time, and a big step forward not just for Rolex, but for those working in these environments. The name says it all. “Milgauss” comes from mille (one thousand) and gauss , the unit used to measure magnetic fields—straightforward, functional, and very Rolex. With scientists at CERN and beyond actually wearing the Milgauss in the field, the watch quickly cemented its place as a true tool piece—built with purpose, but carrying that unmistakable bit of character that still makes it stand out today. At hand we have a reference 1019—the second generation of the Milgauss. This example comes with a strong, well-preserved case and a clean, smooth bezel. The silver dial features the typical vertical brushing, with a warm yellow patina developing on the plots and hands. A subtle splash of red on the “Milgauss” text and seconds hand adds just the right amount of contrast. The watch is paired with an Oyster bracelet (ref. 78360), fitted with a clasp stamped “J7” and correct 580 end links. This fine tool watch with a scientific edge has been fully serviced by our watch maker. One of the more underrated Rolex tool watches—get in touch ! title: Rolex Oysterdate Precision  Silver Star "Stelline " dial ref 6066
description: Every collector knows the feeling: every once in a while, you come across a watch that creates an instant connection. That is exactly how we feel about this humble little Oysterdate. Housed in a charming 30mm Oyster case, this example remains in lovely condition and retains several attractive early details, including the seldom-seen one-sided lug holes, an early patent-signed crown, and a smooth bezel that perfectly complements its understated character. But the real star — quite literally — is the dial. The lovely preserved silvered patina dial features no luminous material, a black Rolex Oysterdate text, and a wonderful combination of dagger and star-shaped hour markers at 6 and 9 o’clock. We absolutely love it. Rolex used these charming star indexes only sparingly throughout its history, making them a highly desirable detail among collectors today. They are perhaps best known from the legendary Ref. 6062, Rolex’s grail-worthy triple-calendar moonphase, produced for only a brief period during the 1950s. Italian collectors affectionately nicknamed the model “Stelline,” meaning “little stars,” a name inspired by these distinctive markers. It is a nickname we are more than happy to borrow for this delightful Oysterdate. Similar star indexes can also be found on the equally rare Ref. 8171 “Padellone,” another celebrated triple-calendar moonphase model, as well as on certain early time-only Bubbleback, or “Ovetto,” references. Although the dial is certainly not perfect, showing some honest age and light patina across its surface, we find these imperfections absolutely perfect. They give the watch character, warmth, and the kind of authenticity that simply cannot be replicated. As if the dial was not charming enough already, Rolex fitted this watch with a striking red date disc and elegant dauphine hands, details that elevate the entire appearance and make this little Oysterdate an absolute stunner. We have paired it with one of our steel straight end-link bracelets, a combination that feels wonderfully period-correct and gives the watch an effortlessly cool vintage presence on the wrist. The watch and its hand wound movement has been fully serviced by our watch maker. While the watches that inspired its nickname occupy the very top tier of Rolex collecting, this Oysterdate offers a wonderful opportunity to enjoy one of the brand’s most charming and unusual dial designs in a far more understated package. Small in size but overflowing with charm, this Oysterdate reminds us that true charisma has never been measured in millimetres. title: Tudor Submariner No Date Black Snowflake SWISS only dial with original box and paper ref 7016/0
description: Introduced in 1969, the Tudor Submariner "Snowflake" is a legendary watch design featuring distinctive angular hands and square hour markers. Originally created to maximize legibility for professional divers, this iconic aesthetic has since become the cornerstone of Tudor’s modern identity. The Snowflake design was born from a close collaboration between Tudor and the French Navy (Marine Nationale), which requested a highly legible dive watch for use in murky, deep-water conditions. Standard Rolex "Mercedes" hands could be difficult to distinguish in low-light environments. The angular, flat surfaces of the Snowflake hands allowed for a generous application of luminous material, ensuring that the hour and minute hands were easily distinguishable from one another. The introduction of the Snowflake hands, along with the square hour markers, coincided with Tudor's transition from the Rose logo to the Shield logo, helping the brand step out of Rolex's shadow and establish its own utilitarian identity. This particular black-dial example boasts several highly desirable and rare features. The earliest Snowflakes are what collectors refer to as "SWISS only" dials, due to "SWISS" being the only text printed between the hash marks at six o’clock. These dials can be found in both black and, much more rarely, blue. The blue dials were introduced first, around 1969 (approximately in the 62xxxx serial range), followed shortly thereafter by the black dials. Black-dial examples are generally found within the 74xxxx to 815xxx serial range, while blue dials are typically associated with the earlier 62xxxx range. The case on this watch is superb. We rarely use the term "unpolished" and prefer to let the photographs speak for themselves, allowing you to form your own opinion. Just look at the shoulders on this beauty. The bezel insert has faded to a gorgeous midnight blue and is the highly sought-after "Kissing 40" variation, so named because the font is so thick that the numerals 4 and 0 actually touch one another. The dial displays the familiar and entirely sympathetic "bubbling" often seen on Snowflake dials. This is an extremely common characteristic, and many dials were replaced by Tudor during routine servicing as a result.The lume collar has gotten a lovely yellow colour over the years. The hands have been "stabilised," meaning that a watchmaker applied a form of lacquer during a service to secure the original lume. This is also a very common period-correct practice, as the wide Snowflake hands often lost lume over decades of use. The watch is fitted with a lovely folded Oyster reference 9315 bracelet with 380 end links and the famous "Pateted" dive extension. This refers to a well-known and highly collectible spelling error found on vintage Rolex and Tudor dive extensions. Instead of "PATENTED," the clasp was stamped "PATETED," omitting the letter "N." What was once a simple factory error has become a prized detail among vintage watch enthusiasts. The watch

title: Heuer Autavia Black Dial ref 7763C Compressor Case
description: The story of the Heuer Autavia is one of evolution—from dashboard instruments to the wrist—spanning decades of motorsport and aviation heritage. Its name itself, a contraction of AUTomobile and AVIAtion, already hints at its purpose. First introduced in 1933 as a dashboard timer, the Autavia was designed for both sectors. It wasn’t until 1962 that Jack Heuer reimagined it as a wristwatch chronograph—marking the beginning of one of Heuer’s most iconic lines. From there, it quickly became associated with the golden era of Formula 1, worn by drivers such as Jo Siffert, Mario Andretti, and Gilles Villeneuve. The example offered here is a late 1960s reference 7763C, housed in a 40 mm case produced by Ervin Piquerez S.A.—better known for its “compressor” cases. This clever construction was designed to improve water resistance, using increasing external pressure to further compress the case gaskets. In other words, the deeper you went, the tighter it sealed—a beautiful piece of engineering from the era. The case remains in great condition and is fitted with a finely toothed rotating bezel, which has developed a subtle fade towards a soft blue hue—adding just the right amount of character. Its reverse panda dial offers a wonderful contrast, with two sub-dials set against a black background. The crisp white chronograph seconds hand adds a touch of sportiness, while the lume has aged to a warm yellow tone, giving the watch a balanced and harmonious appearance.The watch is fitted by one of our Bulang and sons leather straps of which we think as a nice match . Powered by the reliable hand-wound Valjoux 7730 movement, this chronograph has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready to be worn and enjoyed. A piece that captures the spirit of an era—where function, design, and motorsport heritage came together in the most effortless way ! Created to commemorate Rolex’s 40th anniversary, the Datejust represented a significant milestone in watchmaking history. It was the world’s first self-winding, waterproof wristwatch to feature a date display that changed instantaneously at midnight. Unlike purpose-built sports models such as the Submariner, designed for diving, or the Daytona, developed for motorsport enthusiasts, the Datejust was conceived as a versatile and refined timepiece suitable for everyday wear. Its timeless design, practicality, and elegance established the blueprint for the modern dress watch and helped make it one of Rolex’s most celebrated creations. The reference 16234 was introduced in 1988 and remained in production until 2005. The present example features the classic 36 mm Oyster case with a fluted white-gold bezel, both preserved in excellent condition without lug holes .What truly sets this watch apart is its beautiful non-luminous salmon dial, a highly attractive and sought-after configuration that we have always particularly appreciated for its warmth and understated elegance. Combining a desirable salmon dial, classic Datejust proportions, and excellent overall condition, this reference 16234 is a charming and versatile Rolex that will look as appropriate today as it did when it left the factory. title: Rolex Day-Date 1803 Khanjar Sigma Champagne Dial
description: The Rolex Day-Date, introduced in 1956, marked a significant milestone in watchmaking as the world’s first wristwatch to display both the date and the day of the week fully spelled out on the dial. Positioned at the very top of the Rolex catalogue, the Day-Date has exclusively been produced in precious metals — including 18k yellow, white, or rose gold, as well as platinum — reinforcing its status as the brand’s ultimate flagship model! The present watch is a classic 36 mm 18k yellow gold reference 1803, featuring a beautifully preserved case and crisp fluted bezel. While the watch itself is undeniably elegant, the true highlight of this example is undoubtedly its dial!! It features what is arguably the quintessential Day-Date configuration: a sunburst champagne dial with contrasting black printed text, enhanced by a Sigma designation at six o’clock — denoting that the hands and hour markers are crafted from gold. Most notably, the dial proudly bears a rare red Omani Khanjar emblem, adding a fascinating layer of historical significance and collectability. For those less familiar with the emblem, the Omani Khanjar is a traditional ceremonial dagger and one of the most important national symbols of Oman, representing pride, heritage, and status. From the 1970s onward, Qaboos bin Said al Said became widely known for commissioning specially ordered watches adorned with the royal Khanjar crest, either printed on the dial or engraved on the case back. These pieces were typically gifted to high-ranking military officers, diplomats, loyal advisers, and prominent figures within the Sultan’s inner circle, giving them both exceptional rarity and strong historical importance. Many of these special commissions were supplied through Asprey of New Bond Street in London, the Sultan’s official jeweller during the era. Today, Asprey-delivered Khanjar-signed Rolex watches are regarded among the most collectible and desirable special-order vintage Rolex models ever produced, with well-preserved examples becoming increasingly difficult to source. This elegant Day-Date, together with its slow-set movement, has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready to be enjoyed for many years to come. title: Lemania Chronograph cal 28.9 Black Military Dial
description: Alfred Lugrin, a highly skilled watchmaker who trained at Jaeger-LeCoultre, founded his workshop in 1884 in Switzerland’s Vallée de Joux — a region long regarded as the heart of traditional Swiss watchmaking. From the very beginning, the company specialized in producing highly complicated pocket watch movements, including repeaters, chronographs, and precision stopwatches. Between 1928 and 1930, the company officially adopted the name "Lemania Watch Co.," inspired by Lac Léman, the French name for Lake Geneva. During the economic hardships of the Great Depression, Lemania joined forces with Omega and Tissot to form the SSIH group (Société Suisse pour l’Industrie Horlogère), a move that helped secure the future of all three brands. Within the group, Lemania became the primary movement supplier to Omega, a partnership that would go on to shape some of the most important chronographs ever produced. Throughout the 1940s and 1950s, Lemania developed a series of legendary calibres, most notably the celebrated CH27 movement, later known at Omega as the Calibre 321. This movement would go on to power the Omega Speedmaster and eventually became the first and only mechanical chronograph movement flight-qualified by NASA for manned space missions. From the 1950s through the 1970s, Lemania also established itself as the sole manufacturer of wrist chronographs issued to the British Armed Forces, including highly regarded models supplied to the Royal Navy Fleet Air Arm and the Royal Air Force, cementing the brand’s reputation for precision, reliability, and true tool-watch functionality. Offered here is a handsome Lemania two-register chronograph from the 1930s. The watch features a 37 mm case with a snap-back caseback and olive-shaped pushers, all preserved in fine condition. The rare black dial is particularly attractive, featuring a mileage scale along the outer rim, cream-coloured Arabic numerals, and a distinctive snail-style Base 1000 scale. The elegant white leaf-shaped hands complete the beautifully balanced design. This fine chronograph is powered by the hand-wound Lemania Calibre 28.9 and has been fully serviced by our watchmaker. Early chronographs from historically important manufacturers remain remarkably undervalued in today's market, in our view. Finding this level of rarity, character, and style at such an accessible price point is becoming increasingly difficult. For the collector seeking something beyond the usual suspects, this Lemania offers a tremendous amount of watch for the money. title: Rolex Oyster 6282 Cream Boiler Gauge Swiss Only Dial
description: In 1926 — now 100 years ago— Rolex Oyster marked a true turning point in watchmaking history. Developed by founder Hans Wilsdorf, it became the world’s first waterproof and dust proof wristwatch. The name “Oyster” was chosen to reflect its construction: a hermetically sealed case with screw-down bezel, case back, and crown, working much like an oyster shell to protect the movement from water, dust, and external elements. This pioneering design was also patented by Rolex, establishing a new standard in case engineering and laying the foundation for the brand’s reputation for durability and precision. The watch we have here is a seldom-seen reference 6282, a significant time-only model produced between 1952 and 1958. It represents the essence of Rolex’s early post-war philosophy — robust, functional watchmaking focused on reliability and water resistance, before the full transition toward automatic movements that would later define the brand. The 34 mm case is well preserved and retains a smooth bezel, presenting a clean and honest vintage profile. The true highlight, however, is the exceptional dial. Over time, it has developed a rich, deep cream patina across the surface, adding warmth and character. The layout is highly unusual, featuring distinctive boat-shaped hour markers — with a double marker at 12 o’clock — positioned toward the centre of the dial and aligned with a row of raised circular indices. A fine printed seconds track frames the design, while the absence of lume keeps the aesthetic pure and understated. As an early execution, the lower dial reads “Shock Resisting,” whereas later versions were marked “Precision.” Completing the look are elegant leaf-shaped hands with a blued sweeping seconds hand. Due to its distinctive appearance, we have affectionately nicknamed it the “Boil Gauge” dial. We have paired this charming Oyster with one of our straight-end link bracelets, which we feel gives it a perfectly period-correct and balanced wrist presence. The watch and its hand-wound movement have been fully serviced by our watchmaker and are ready to be enjoyed for years to come. An honest and highly attractive early Rolex, rich in texture, detail, and history, get in touch! title: Rolex GMT-Master 1675/8 Unqiue Brown Khanjar Nipple Dial with Rolex Service Papers
description: The Rolex GMT-Master has always held a very special place in the world of collecting, but every now and then a watch appears that goes far beyond the already legendary status of the model itself. This 1974 Rolex GMT-Master 1675/8 is exactly that watch. At first glance, it already carries everything we love about the yellow gold GMT: the warm brown nipple dial, the rich brown insert, and the unmistakable glamour of one of Rolex’s most charismatic sports watches. It has that irresistible mix of elegance, confidence and jet-set charm that makes the gold GMT-Master such a fascinating watch in the metal. But what transforms this example into something truly extraordinary is the large Khanjar crest seen above 6 o’clock on the dial. From the 1970s onwards, Sultan Qaboos of Oman became known for personally commissioning watches that were enhanced with his royal emblem, the Khanjar crest, either on the dial or the caseback. Many of these watches were presented as gifts to trusted advisors, military figures and close relations, making them not only highly collectible, but also deeply historical objects. During the 1970s, many of these special-order watches were delivered to the Sultan through the family jeweller John Asprey of New Bond Street in London. Watches supplied through Asprey have become some of the most celebrated Omani-issued pieces in the world of collecting, with Rolex sports models standing out as the absolute rarest and most elusive examples to find with a Khanjar crest. Omani Khanjar-signed watches have long been among the most desirable and historically important special-order pieces in the world of vintage Rolex collecting. To find such a crest on any sports Rolex is exceptional. To find it on a gold GMT-Master 1675/8 is on another level entirely. In fact, this watch is believed to be one of only two known examples in this configuration, making it without question one of the rarest GMT-Masters in existence, and very possibly the rarest gold GMT-Master ever to surface. That alone would make it important, but in the metal it becomes something even more special. It is one of those watches that immediately stops you in your tracks. The striking combination of the warm matte brown dial with the bold Khanjar crest creates a presence that is impossible to ignore. It combines the elegance and jet-set appeal of the gold GMT with the mystique and historical importance of one of the most celebrated dial signatures in the vintage watch world. The result is not just rare, but breathtakingly attractive. Collectors will know just how elusive Khanjar watches are, especially when found on highly collectible Rolex sports models. This example stands at the very top of that category. Not only because of its rarity, but because watches like this almost never appear, and once they disappear into important collections, they are rarely seen again. It is exactly the kind of watch that lives in books, in stories, and in the dreams of seasoned collectors. Condition

title: Rolex Day-Date 18038 Petrol Blue Stella Dial in 18k Yellow Gold
description: Since its official debut in 1956, the Day-Date has been produced exclusively in precious metals. As the flagship model of the Genevan manufacturer, it has long been synonymous with success, frequently seen on the wrists of heads of state, royalty, and other influential figures. Most Day-Dates were fitted with discreet, conservative dials—after all, most buyers of this model preferred elegance over extravagance. But Rolex made a notable exception to this unwritten rule: beginning in the 1970s, they introduced bright, high-gloss lacquered dials known today as “Stella” dials. At the time, these bold colours were not widely embraced, precisely because they attracted attention. As a result, production numbers remained low, making them highly sought after today. A wide array of colours is known—yellow, green, orange, red ,pink and multiple shades of blue, some embellished with gemstones, and produced across different metals. They also span various generations: from the early 18xx “pie-pan” versions to the later 18xxx models with flat dials. The manufacturing process was exceptionally labor-intensive. Each dial was spray-painted and then oven-baked to set the pigment. This cycle was repeated multiple times until the desired depth of colour and finish was achieved. Afterward, the dial was polished and coated with a clear lacquer. This final step created the distinctive effect where the printed text appears to float above the glossy surface, reminiscent of the porcelain-dial Daytonas. The example at hand is a second-series reference 18038, featuring a light blue—what we prefer to call “petrol blue”—Stella dial with diamond-set hour markers, and beautifully aged yellow tritium plots and fine gold printed text.The day disc is in English. The case is in outstanding condition, boasting thick, well-defined lugs and a sharp fluted bezel. The President bracelet is a reference 8385 with solid end links, a concealed clasp, and fits wrists up to 18 cm.This cool blue Day-Date has been fully serviced by our watchmaker. title: Rolex Oyster Perpetual Date 1500 Taupe Singer Proto/Test Dial in 14k Yellow Gold
description: We always try to offer you something uncommon or seldom seen — and today we have something special to propose once again. At hand is an unusual 14 kt yellow gold Oyster Perpetual Date, made for the British market. Eighteen-karat gold watches were much more expensive to import into certain countries, such as the USA and the UK. For that reason, many brands also offered 14 kt gold models. The most famous examples are the Rolex hand-wound Daytona models, where a 14 kt example can have a huge price difference compared to an 18 kt gold version nowadays — sometimes reaching differences of several hundred thousand! The case of this reference 1500 model, with its smooth bezel, is in excellent condition. Rolex decided to engrave the full serial number of this example inside the case back — a very uncommon feature. It is known that Rolex only did this for special deliveries, such as the famed military Submariners, the first “experimental” Sea-Dwellers (given to professional deep-sea divers for testing), unique pieces, and watches made for important collectors like the late Sultan Qaboos bin Said Al Said, who ordered a number of watches featuring the “Khanjar” coat of arms. The soleil-finished grey non lumed dial is another extremely uncommon feature. In fact, we have never seen another exactly like this. The dial resembles features like these unusual markers, very close in style to those made by the famous dial maker Singer, who produced the dials for what is arguably one of the most collectible watches of all time — the Daytona Exotic Dials. As the story goes, around a decade ago, a number of books containing loose dials were discovered — “study” dials from Singer, created as proposals to various brands including Universal Genève, Omega, and, as mentioned, Rolex. Some of these proposals were eventually used by Rolex in models such as the Daytona as well as in Datejust and other dressier models from that era. If you search “Rolex Singer prototype dials” online, a whole world opens up that helps illustrate what we are referring to. We have also previously had some rarer Datejusts with this feature and shared a small write-up on those as well over HERE We believe this dial was more a proto as “test for the market, meant as a way of testing the waters. description: The name Calatrava traces its origins to medieval Spain, referring both to a fortress in the Castile region and to a chivalric order founded in 1157, established to defend it. The Order of Calatrava adopted a distinctive emblem—a red Greek cross with fleur-de-lis tips—a symbol that would later take on an entirely new significance in the world of watchmaking. In 1887, Patek Philippe selected this cross as part of its official trademark, registering it alongside the name Patek Philippe & Cie . The exact reasoning behind this choice has never been clearly documented. It may simply have been the strength and elegance of the design, or perhaps a deeper symbolic link to values such as tradition, discipline, and longevity. Whatever the case, the Calatrava cross appeared only sparingly on the brand’s early watches. Notably, Calatrava was not initially used as a model designation. It was only in the 1980s that the name formally entered Patek Philippe’s catalogue. Nevertheless, collectors and historians retrospectively adopted the term to describe the brand’s refined, time-only dress watches of the 1930s—most famously beginning with Reference 96—thereby establishing the Calatrava as a cornerstone of Patek Philippe’s design language. Since the introduction of the Calatrava in 1932, Patek Philippe has produced well over 100 distinct references. The collection has evolved continuously, encompassing a wide range of executions, from classic time-only models and officer-style cases to more recent and complex interpretations such as Annual Calendar and Pilot Travel Time models. Offered here is a beautiful time-only Calatrava, reference 3513, crafted in 18k white gold. It features a clean, flat bezel, a snap-back 31 mm case, and a small winding crown set with a black-topped cabochon. The watch is fitted with a finely crafted integrated 18k white gold bracelet, finished by hand with a striking hammered effect—a detail that speaks volumes about the level of craftsmanship involved. The bracelet comfortably fits wrists up to approximately 18–18.5 cm and is secured by an elegant clasp adorned with the iconic Calatrava cross. The dial is finished in a soft silver tone, complemented by black painted Roman numerals and simple black stick hands, with no luminous material—pure, understated elegance. An elegant and increasingly elusive white-gold Calatrava, this reference perfectly embodies Patek Philippe's enduring philosophy of understated luxury and timeless design. An elegant addition to any serious collection! title: Rolex GMT-Master 1675 Tropical Brown Gilt Chapter Ring Dial Pointed Crown Guard Case
description: The Rolex GMT-Master ref. 1675 is one of the most iconic and recognisable vintage watches ever produced. Manufactured from 1959 to 1980, its 21-year production run makes it one of the longest-standing references in Rolex history, resulting in a wide array of highly collectible variations. The model achieved legendary status through its association with Pan Am pilots, and NASA astronaut Jack Swigert of the Apollo 13 mission. Presented here is an early 1960s example featuring the so-called pointed crown guard (PCG) case. The Pointed Crown Guards, often referred to by Italian collectors as “Cornino” (“little horns”), are a hallmark of the earliest GMT-Master 1675 models produced between 1959 and approximately 1964. When Rolex transitioned from the original ref. 6542—which had no crown guards—to the 1675, it experimented with case shapes. The PCG is the most sought-after case design of that period. Unlike the thicker, rounded crown guards found on later models, the PCG tapers to a sharp point, giving the watch a slimmer and more technical aesthetic. The case remains in excellent condition, retaining strong proportions. It is fitted with a slightly faded red-back “Pepsi” bezel insert, where the blue has softened to a washed, denim-like tone, while the red remains vibrant. The dial is a so-called gilt “chapter ring” version. Unlike later dials, where the text is printed on the surface, a gilt dial is created through a complex galvanic process. The dial begins as a brass plate, with the text and markings applied in clear lacquer. It is then treated so that the surrounding surface turns black, leaving the underlying brass visible—resulting in a rich, glossy, gold-toned text with remarkable depth. The “chapter ring” refers to the fine gilt circle connecting the minute markers along the outer edge of the dial. Over time, this example has developed a warm brown patina—referred to by collectors as a “tropical dial.” A highly sought-after characteristic, it gives the watch a unique warmth and character. Furthermore, the dial features smaller lume plots, typical for chapter ring versions, with correct period lume that reacts with a bright green glow under UV light—present both on the dial and the handset. The watch is fitted with a folded Jubilee bracelet, reference 6251H, with end links stamped 55 and a clasp dated 1/65. The watch has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready for many years of enjoyment. title: Rolex Day-Date 18078 Green Khanjar Champagne Dial Bark Finish in 18k Yellow Gold
description: The Rolex Day-Date, introduced in 1956, marked a significant milestone in watchmaking as the world’s first wristwatch to display both the date and the day of the week fully spelled out on the dial. Positioned at the very top of the Rolex catalogue, the Day-Date has exclusively been produced in precious metals — including 18k yellow, white, or Everose gold, as well as platinum — reinforcing its status as the brand’s ultimate flagship model. The model became closely associated with the iconic “President” bracelet, a semi-circular three-link design created specifically for the Day-Date’s launch. While the bracelet itself carried the “President” name, the nickname soon became synonymous with the entire watch. The Day-Date’s association with influential world leaders further elevated its legendary status. Dwight D. Eisenhower famously received a Rolex from the brand, while Lyndon B. Johnson was often seen wearing a yellow gold Day-Date during his presidency. Over the decades, the model has become an enduring symbol of prestige, success, and leadership, worn by presidents, executives, and cultural icons around the world. This particular example features several highly desirable and seldom-seen characteristics. It is preserved in the rare reference 18078 configuration, distinguished by its hand-finished “bark” decoration — a textured motif applied to both the bezel and President bracelet, designed to resemble the natural grain of tree bark. This intricate finish gives the watch a striking and unmistakably luxurious appearance. The champagne dial is beautifully balanced and elevated further by an exceptionally rare green Omani Khanjar and crown signature printed on the left side of the dial. Additional details include a finely printed railroad minute track, warm cream-coloured lume plots, and an English day disc. For those unfamiliar with the symbol, the Omani Khanjar is a traditional curved dagger worn ceremonially in Oman, representing heritage, honour, and national pride. During the 1970s onward, Qaboos bin Said al Said became renowned for commissioning specially ordered watches featuring the royal Khanjar crest, either printed on the dial or engraved on the case back. These watches were typically presented to senior military officials, diplomats, trusted advisers, and members of the Sultan’s inner circle, making them objects of both extraordinary rarity and important historical significance. Many of these bespoke commissions were supplied through Asprey of New Bond Street, London, the Sultan’s preferred jeweller during the period. Watches retailed through Asprey — particularly Rolex models bearing the Khanjar emblem — have since become some of the most coveted and elusive special-order timepieces in the world of vintage Rolex collecting. title: Rolex Submariner 5513 MilSub with Rolex Service Card
description: Say “MilSub” to a watch collector and you might just see them go weak at the knees—or momentarily lost for words. The Rolex Military Submariner, or “MilSub,” was produced in the 1970s in extremely small quantities (just over 1,000 pieces), of which only a few hundred are believed to survive today. It’s no surprise these watches are considered true grails—often commanding between €200k and €500k depending on condition and provenance. But what’s the story behind these rare Submariners? Although produced in the 1970s, the MilSub’s origins trace back to World War II and the rise of underwater combat operations. The Italians were early pioneers in this field, using Panerai watches—interestingly manufactured by Rolex at the time. Great Britain soon followed, commissioning purpose-built watches capable of withstanding prolonged underwater missions. After the war, this evolved into ongoing diving operations within the British Ministry of Defence (MoD), which required reliable, purpose-built wristwatches. By 1957, the MoD approached Rolex with a clear set of specifications. Rolex responded by adapting its Submariner with fixed spring bars, a larger bezel for operation with gloves, and dials using tritium lume (marked by the encircled “T”) instead of the more hazardous radium. For a brief period, the MoD turned to Omega, commissioning military versions of the Seamaster 300. However, in the early 1970s, they returned to Rolex—likely due to the superior water resistance offered by Rolex’s screw-down crown system. One requirement carried over from the Omega designs was the use of “sword hands,” providing greater lume surface and improved underwater legibility. The Submariner reference 5513 was subsequently modified to meet these specifications. Changes included fixed bars, a fully graduated 60-minute bezel insert, a matte dial, and the distinctive sword hands. Over the course of the 1970s, these watches underwent subtle evolutions. Early examples were marked “5513” between the lugs, followed by versions bearing both “5513” and “5517,” with the final series marked solely “5517.” These watches were issued primarily to two branches of the British military: Army (W10 designation) Case backs were engraved with: W10 (MoD code for the Army) 6645 (NATO code for time-measuring instruments) 99 (NATO country code for the UK) 923-7697 (NATO code for divers’ watches) Broad Arrow marking Issue number and year Royal Navy (0552 designation) Case backs were engraved with: 0552 (Royal Navy service code) 923-7697 (NATO code for divers’ watches) Broad Arrow marking Issue number and year Inside the case back of a correct MilSub, one would typically find engravings indicating the model reference, the date of manufacture for the case or case back, and—depending on the batch—the serial number matching the case. title: Rolex Chronograph ref. 4500 Pulsations Dial
description: The Rolex Chronograph ref. 4500, introduced around 1945, is a historically significant and rare example of one of the earliest waterproof Oyster chronographs, often referred to as the “Monoblocco” due to its one-piece case design. It marked a key design shift toward the later “modern” Daytona, with a 36mm size, straight lugs, and a two-register layout powered by a Valjoux 23–based movement. The case on this example is in excellent condition, featuring a screw-down back, pump-style pushers, and its original winding crown still attached. The true showstopper is the extremely rare pulsations dial. The pulso meter scale was primarily designed for medical professionals, namely doctors. pulsations -signed Rolex chronographs are extraordinarily rare, with approximately 50 pieces known across all metals and references. The lineage of these “medical” chronographs includes very early references such as 2023 and 2057 from the late 1920s, the “Bariletto” reference 3525 in steel during the 1940s, as well as references 4048, 4062, 4099, 4537 (in stainless steel or stainless steel and gold), and the ref. 4500 in gold. In the 1950s, the pulso meter scale appeared on some examples of the 6034 and 6234 in stainless steel and gold, followed by a handful of ref. 6238s with the scale inside the indexes, and finally around ten examples of the ref. 6239 Daytona in steel. After this period, Rolex ceased producing pulsometer dials for over 60 years, and they remain absent in modern production. This particular dial features a French-language pulso meter scale in blue (‘Gradué pour 30 pulsations’), suggesting it was likely made on special request for a French-speaking doctor. Such dials were extremely rare and difficult to produce in batches due to very low demand. The dial also features a fine black seconds track, two sub dials, applied Arabic numerals, and arrowhead hour markers, all showing pleasing patina. It is topped with clean non-lumed stick-style hands, completing a truly remarkable vintage chronograph. The watch is paired with an Oyster riveted-style ref 7206 bracelet, with end links marked 60 and a clasp stamped 1/60. This fine doctor’s chronograph and its hand-wound Cal. VLJX.23 movement have been fully serviced by our watchmaker. One of approximately 50 known pulsations examples across all references and a true collector’s find—reach out to secure this rare doctor’s Rolex chronograph! description: The Omega Cosmic Ref. 2486 represents one of the brand’s most intriguing yet quietly underappreciated achievements of the mid-20th century. Featuring a full calendar complication, it once stood among the most sophisticated offerings in Omega’s lineup, reflecting the technical ambition of the era. Calendar-equipped Cosmics often fly under the radar, frequently overshadowed by more complex perpetual calendar models. Yet their charm lies precisely in this balance of practicality, elegance, and mechanical interest. This particular example elevates the reference even further, distinguished by an exceptionally rare dial configuration with day and month displays rendered in Farsi (Persian)—a detail seldom encountered and highly desirable among seasoned collectors. Compact in concept yet rich in character, this watch offers the appeal of a calendar complication without the ostentation often associated with larger, more imposing counterparts. A refined and culturally significant piece, it stands as a fascinating alternative to the more celebrated calendar watches of its time. Farsi-dial Omega Cosmics are a recognized category among collectors, yet they were not bespoke commissions. Instead, they originated from a very limited production run intended for the Middle Eastern market. A closer look at the dial reveals an important distinction: rather than the Eastern Arabic numerals commonly seen today, the script is true Farsi, identifiable by the heart-shaped numeral five. Most of these watches were originally delivered to Iran. It is widely believed that the majority were sold in Tehran, then a rapidly modernizing, oil-wealthy capital under the rule of Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. The Omega Cosmic calendar was produced in five round-case references, offered in both 35mm (Refs. 2606, 2471, and 2473) and larger 37mm formats (Refs. 2485 and 2486). Farsi-signed dials are most frequently encountered in the 2606 and 2486 references. The present example features a “jumbo” 37.5mm pink gold-plated case—an era-specific detail that highlights Omega’s broad material offerings at the time, which ranged from stainless steel to gold-plated and solid gold constructions. The pink gold-plated case is in lovely condition and features a snap-back case back, side correctors for the moon phase and calendar functions, elegant lugs, and a thin bezel, allowing the dial to appear even larger on the wrist. The black dial shows some honest age, yet remains highly attractive and sympathetic for a watch dating to the late 1940s. It features the aforementioned Farsi numerals, with matching Farsi calendar displays visible through the dial apertures. Additional details include leaf-shaped hands, a blued hand for the date indication, a small running seconds at six o’clock, and a beautifully rendered moonphase in the same area. title: Audemars Piguet Ultra Thin Dress Watch in 18kt White Gold Silver Diamond Markers Dial
description: The history of Audemars Piguet (AP) is a story of independence and high-end innovation. Founded in 1875, it remains the oldest fine watchmaking manufacturer still in the hands of its founding families—the Audemars and Piguet families. Jules Louis Audemars and Edward Auguste Piguet joined forces in Le Brassus, Switzerland. Audemars focused on creating complex movements, while Piguet handled the final finishing and commercial operations. The brand soon gained fame for miniaturizing complex mechanisms, and in 1892 they developed the world’s first minute repeater wristwatch. Facing the Quartz Crisis in the 1970s, AP took a bold gamble by hiring designer Gérald Genta to create a luxury watch made of steel rather than gold. The result was the iconic Audemars Piguet Royal Oak, with its octagonal bezel and visible screws—ultimately saving the company and creating the luxury steel sports watch category. Together with Vacheron Constantin and Patek Philippe, AP forms part of the so-called “Holy Trinity” of watchmaking. Yet unlike its peers, AP is often considered the most rebellious of the three, blending traditional craftsmanship with avant-garde designs and bold collaborations. This lovely dress watch represents one of the “pre-Royal Oak” specialties of AP: the ultra-thin watches. During the mid-20th century, several watchmakers pushed the boundaries of how thin a mechanical movement could be, allowing watches to become more elegant and lightweight—a “competition” in which AP was a true leader. Here we have a beautiful example: an ultra-thin 18k white gold “time-only” dress watch measuring 31 mm, with small lugs and a delicate thin bezel. The silvered dial features 12 diamond hour markers and elegant stick hands. Without a running seconds hand, the dial offers a certain sense of calm and serenity. This elegant piece is paired with a beautiful Bulang & Sons leather strap, and its ultra-thin movement has been fully serviced by our watchmaker. Interested in this beautiful pre-Audemars Piguet Royal Oak era dress watch? We’re happy to share more details. Built for men who don’t flinch at 50 metres under the Sea level and issued to those who actually earned the right to wear it — the Omega “Big Triangle” Seamaster isn’t just a handsome face, it’s proper military kit . title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Flyback Chronograph 5960P in Platinum Execution Grey dial Full Set
description: The first of a new generation chronographs After an extended period of Patek Philippe producing calendar watches with Valjoux or Lemania base movements, the brand made a significant leap in 2006 with the introduction of a groundbreaking new reference and complication that highlighted their in-house movement within a calendar chronograph. This innovation led to the creation of the elegant yet sporty 5960 in Platinum, an annual calendar “flyback” chronograph. The annual calendar, originally introduced by Patek Philippe in 1996 with reference 5035, offers the functionality of a perpetual calendar but at a lower cost, to make a bridge between a basic calatrava and perpetual. It offers than the same character as the more mature perpetual but with the require to set it manually only once a year in February. With the 5960, Patek Philippe advanced this complication by incorporating a chronograph module, providing a modern alternative to their traditional perpetual chronographs like the 5970/5270. This marked the debut of an in-house chronograph movement and set the stage alongside the Nautilus chronograph 5980, establishing a new classic. Since its launch, various iterations of the 5960 have emerged, but we are excited to present an example in its original configuration: the platinum case model featuring a striking grey soleil dial. This design gives the watch a captivating depth, enhanced by elegant details such as leaf hands, luminous dots, and a sporty monocounter at the 6 o’clock position, complemented by a day/night indicator, power reserve, and an American-style calendar layout. This particular piece dates back to 2010 and comes as a full set being accompanied by its original sale papers, booklets, inner and outer box, delivery box with seal and accessories, including the white gold folding clasp, strap and corrector pin. The watch remains in excellent condition, having been preserved in great condition and seen minimal wrist time. Due to its collectibility and pristine state, having barely been worn, we have decided not to service or open the case yet, but on request of the client will be executed. We see this watch as an undervalued gem, overlooked yet poised to become a future classic due to its outstanding design and historical significance. If this remarkable timepiece resonates with you, we invite you to reach out to our private sales team, to discuss this exceptional Patek Philippe. Over the years, subtle design variations in the dial and bezel have turned each iteration into a collectible in its own right. Unlike many of Rolex’s sport models that gained status-symbol recognition early on, the 1655 flew under the radar for quite some time. What we have here is a standout example of one of the earliest executions: a Mark 2, nicknamed the "Frog Foot" dial, as the coronet resembles a frog’s footprint. Both the case and bezel are in strong, well-preserved condition, and the dial is beautiful, showcasing creamy yellow lume plots with a wonderfully aged tone. Fully serviced by our watchmaker, this Explorer II is ready for everyday wear—or to be tucked into a serious collector’s vault. Among matte-dial vintage Rolex sports models, the 1655 remains one of the coolest—and arguably most underappreciated. This example ticks all the right boxes: a bold faded-orange hand, clean straight seconds, and a warm, even yellow patina. Drop us a message if you're ready to explore this classic “Albino” for yourself—this one’s a gem! Introduced in 1953, it was Rolex’s first commercially available watch with a rotating bezel—a feature often mistakenly credited to the Submariner—and the first sports model offered in Rolesor, the combination of steel and gold. By blending practical functionality with sporty elegance, the Turn-O-Graph laid the groundwork for what we now recognize as the modern tool watch. Its rotating bezel would go on to inspire defining features of some of Rolex’s most iconic sports watches, including the Submariner, and GMT-Master. Eventually, the Turn-O-Graph became integrated into the Datejust line, serving as its sporty variant. The example we have here is a classic 36 mm steel variant, featuring a turnable bezel in excellent condition and a beautifully preserved case. The stepped, pie-pan style silver dial is highlighted by striking black-topped hour markers, creating a sharp contrast and timeless appeal. The company, now known as IWC Schaffhausen, is a renowned watch manufacturer that has expanded into wristwatches and innovative materials while remaining true to its engineering-focused philosophy. The IWC Portofino collection evolved from a design inspired by a classic pocket watch and has since become one of IWC's most successful lines, known for its understated elegance and timeless aesthetics. The full Portofino collection was officially launched in 1984, named after the picturesque Italian fishing village to evoke the spirit of la dolce vita . Turning the watch over, you’ll find a striking “Khanjar” engraved on the case back. A khanjar is a traditional Omani ceremonial dagger with a curved, J-shaped blade. Worn by men as a symbol of status, masculinity, and national pride, it forms part of the traditional Omani dress for formal, religious, and celebratory occasions. Often ornately decorated, the khanjar is also the national emblem of Oman. This watch was gifted to someone special by the late Sultan Qaboos bin Said al Said. In the watch-collecting world, it is well known that the Sultan was an avid admirer of fine timepieces, and quite a number of Rolex, Cartier, and IWC models bearing this emblem are documented. This Portofino comes on its original IWC leather strap, fitted with a steel IWC pin buckle. The watch includes its original inner and outer boxes, with the outer box once again featuring a red Khanjar printed on top. It also comes with its original guarantee card and a “thank you” card in Arabic. The watch has been fully checked and regulated by our watchmaker. title: Rolex Submariner 6205 Small Crown "First Submariner"
description: The 1950s proved to be a defining era for Rolex, highlighted by the introduction of some of its most legendary models: the Submariner, GMT-Master, Day-Date, and Explorer lines. As scuba diving gained traction among adventurers and professionals alike, Rolex recognized the growing demand for a dependable dive watch to help monitor time spent underwater and reduce the risk of decompression sickness, also known as “the bends.” There was also a need for a reliable timing device to track the remaining “breathing time.” This vision culminated in the creation of the Submariner—a timepiece that would come to represent not only technical excellence and rugged reliability but also timeless design. The Rolex Submariner reference 6205 was introduced in 1954 as one of the earliest Submariner models, alongside references 6204 and 6200. The 6205 was produced for only about a year, making it a rare and highly sought-after collector's item. As Rolex themselves put it in the book Oyster Perpetual Submariner: The Watch That Unlocked the Deep , just 810 examples were produced. To put that in perspective: approximately 2,800 reference 6538 "Big Crown" Submariners were made. A signficant innovation of the 6205 was the introduction of the "Submariner" name on the dial, a feature that has remained on all subsequent Submariner models, so maybe we can conclude this is the “real “first Submariner! The “ no depth rating “ dial is still in nice condition, with the original pencil and “lollipop” seconds hands present. Although the hands have been re-lumed in the pas they still look charming. The 37.5 mm “small crown “ case stays in nice condition .The so-called “no-hash” bezel insert remains on the watch in unmolested condition, though we believe the bezel itself is a later replacement and has been paired with one of our leather straps. This super early “Neanderthaler” Sub has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready to join a Submariner-themed collection. We've enjoyed this watch for some time, and it has truly grown on us. Get in touch. title: Blancpain Fifty Fathoms "No Rad" Date
description: The Fifty Fathoms was originally developed in collaboration with the French Navy’s elite combat divers—and its legacy lives on today, even in modern pop culture, thanks to the recent Blancpain × Swatch Bioceramic Scuba collection. But if you’ve got the Swatch, you really need to experience the original. This is a desirable 41mm example in beautiful, honest condition—exactly what we love to see. The name Fifty Fathoms might sound unusual, but it refers to a British unit of measurement. A fathom equals about six feet, so fifty fathoms translates to roughly 91 meters—close to 300 feet—the maximum depth divers could reach with the technology available at the time. Fifty Fathoms watches have seen serious military use over the decades, trusted by forces from France, Germany, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Finland, and most famously, the U.S. Navy. This particular version is the highly sought-after "No Radiations" model, often nicknamed the “No-Rad.” What makes it special? That iconic yellow-and-red crossed-out radiation symbol on the dial. It signified that no radium was used in the luminous material—a move made in the early 1960s as the health risks of radium became more widely known. The “No Rad” logo offered peace of mind to both professional and recreational divers. Due to their historical significance—and that instantly recognizable symbol—these models are now highly prized by collectors. Blancpain has even released tribute editions of the Fifty Fathoms No Rad, cementing its place in the brand’s history. title: Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Ref. 6001ST
description: The reference 6001 is a watch you’re unlikely to have encountered before. It’s not a Royal Oak, designed by Jean-Fred Meylan (not Gérald Genta), and visually, it shares little in common with any other Audemars Piguet model, aside from its small tapisserie dial. Fewer than 350 pieces are believed to have been produced between 1974 and 1978, after which it was replaced by the reference 6005, which bears a much closer resemblance to the Royal Oak (though it’s not called that!). The 6001 was a bold experiment, introduced during the height of the "quartz revolution." In the end, Audemars Piguet embraced quartz technology, using a modified Beta 21 movement from Omega, known as the 'megaquartz' for its remarkable 2,359,296 vibrations per second. This movement would lose or gain no more than one second per month. That small pusher near the crown? It’s used to fine-tune the time by correcting that single second. The "rounded yet octagonal" case has soft, flowing edges, far removed from the angular lines of the original Royal Oak. It has a very 1970s, almost Star Wars-esque vibe mixed with Royal Oak influences—a design that feels both futuristic and retro at the same time! The 35 x 40 mm steel case remains in excellent condition, and the integrated AP bracelet (which fits wrists up to 18 cm) is also in great shape. The signature petite tapisserie dial is in blue, featuring an applied AP logo on the lower half (just as the original Royal Oak 5402 would have had during its era!) with a date at 6 o’clock. The hands are typical of AP’s design, with the first series of Royal Oak tritium markers. The quartz-driven movement (caliber 2510) has been fully checked by our watchmaker and a fresh battery is fitted. This is a rare watch from one of the “Holy Trinity” of watch brands. Come on, guys—this is a conversation piece and super cool! Get in touch! title: Smiths "Deluxe" ref 6B/542 Military Watch for the British RAF
description: In the late 1940s and early 1950s, Smiths was commissioned to produce a General Service wristwatch for the British Armed Forces. The British government, concerned about dependence on foreign watch suppliers—something that had proven problematic during World War II—offered Smiths substantial contracts to encourage domestic watch production. However, for reasons unknown, the British Army ultimately chose not to move forward with the order. It wasn’t until the late 1960s that Smiths secured a military contract—this time for the W10 model. These watches were assigned the same 6B/542 stores reference as the Omega navigators’ watch, suggesting they were likely issued to RAF pilots and navigators. This is the rarest Smiths British military watch, and arguably one of the rarest British military watches of all. Approximately 300 of these watches were made and issued to the RAF in 1954, 1955, and 1956—presumably as a test order. This would make sense for a trial run, as the inside of an aircraft cockpit presented a challenging environment for mechanical wristwatches, mainly due to the presence of electromagnetic fields. To combat this, the watches were equipped with an iron dial and a metal dust cover, which together created an effective Faraday cage to shield the movement from electromagnetic interference. This particular Smiths was issued in 1955, as evidenced by its issue number on the case back. The case is in lovely condition, with fixed bars for fitting a single-pass strap—so military personnel had a slimmer chance of losing the watch during duties. This example has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready for new adventures in the years to come. A fun fact about these Smiths Deluxe watches: there were also some non-issued, non-military-marked versions. This particular model, housed in a water-resistant case, was worn by Sir Edmund Hillary during his ascent of Everest (and you thought it was all about Rolex!). The Smiths De Luxe A454 and A460 models, known as the ‘Antarctic’ versions, were supplied to the 1957 British Antarctic expedition, in which Hillary also participated. These models feature a silver-colored dial and a finer outer minute track. These super RARE purpose-built watches hold real history and have a super cool wrist presence, we think. Get in touch! title: IWC Ingenieur SL Jumbo Quartz Black Dial Ref. 3303
description: The IWC Ingenieur was first introduced in 1954 as a tool watch specifically designed for engineers and technicians who needed a timepiece that could withstand magnetic fields and harsh environments. The original model featured a soft iron inner case to protect the movement from magnetic interference. Over the years, while the design has evolved, the Ingenieur has always remained true to its original purpose: a rugged, reliable timepiece built for professionals. In the mid-1970s, IWC enlisted the renowned designer Gerald Genta to update the Ingenieur’s design, resulting in a more modern, fashionable aesthetic. The “Genta” Ingenieur debuted in 1976 and hit stores in 1977, featuring a large case with an integrated bracelet and powered by the automatic c.8541ES movement. Due to its substantial size, the mechanical Ingenieur ref. 1832 quickly earned the affectionate nickname “Fat” Ingenieur. However, despite its innovative design, it struggled to gain market traction, mainly due to its high price and the onset of the "quartz crisis." To adapt, IWC released two quartz versions: the first with the quartz calibre 2405, followed by a slimmer model with the quartz calibre 2250, a more comfortable bracelet, and a refined case design. In 1980, the ref. 3303 replaced the ref. 3003, offering a flatter case and the same quartz calibre 2250. The present watch is a rare and highly sought-after IWC “Genta” Ingenieur reference 3303, featuring a quartz movement. With only 149 examples ever produced, and even fewer appearing on the market, this timepiece is truly a collector's gem! We’re especially fond of the stunning black "waffle dial," a signature design element from IWC that almost resembles carbon fiber. The iconic Genta-designed three-row bracelet is in excellent condition, fitting wrists up to 18.5 cm, and the signature “fish crown” remains intact. The watch has been fully checked by our watchmaker and is fitted with a fresh battery. Reach out to us to learn more about this cool, iconic IWC designed by Genta! title: IWC Da Vinci Perpetual Calendar Silver Dial Ref. IW375803
description: The IWC Da Vinci line emerged in 1969 with the introduction of the very first IWC Da Vinci, equipped with the infamous Beta 21 quartz movement. However, the watch we have at hand is a very different kind of timepiece! The first significant evolution of the collection occurred in 1985 with what is undoubtedly the most famous version: the Da Vinci Perpetual Calendar (Ref. 3750). This model was created under the technical guidance of Kurt Klaus, while Günter Blümlein served as CEO of IWC. The launch of this watch is quite significant, and the context warrants explanation. During the early 1980s, the Swiss watch industry faced massive changes. Interest in quality mechanical timepieces—ranging from simple three-hand watches to complex pieces—was limited to a small group of collectors and enthusiasts. Wearers of mechanical watches were rare and often perceived as “old-school” or “outdated.” While sales representatives from historic brands like IWC attempted to convey the beauty of mechanical movements and the dedication of watchmakers in crafting fine timepieces, clients were captivated by the slim and precise electronic quartz watches. At the Basel Watch Fair in 1985, a new watch was introduced that combined striking design with a complex perpetual calendar chronograph movement (the ancestor of the watch we have today): the Da Vinci Perpetual Calendar (Ref. 3750). This watch, the first in the new Da Vinci collection, is the result of designer Hano Burtscher’s vision, featuring a round design with articulated swivel lugs. More importantly, this watch symbolizes the resurgence of complex mechanical movements. At the end of the 1970s, Kurt Klaus developed a perpetual calendar module that allowed all settings to be made via the crown, easily attachable to almost any movement—from a simple three-hander to a chronograph. Our watch is based on this design language and movement, featuring a nicely sized 41mm steel case with “mushroom” pushers. There is a lot to take in when looking at the dial: it features a white background with painted Arabic numeral hour markers, a 12-hour chronograph, a perpetual calendar displaying the day, date, month, and four-digit year, as well as a moonphase! All of this is protected by a sapphire crystal. The moonphase has a lovely sparkle, a little detail we truly appreciate. All settings can be adjusted using the crown at 3 o’clock—a very ingenious design! This lovely IWC comes on a Bulang & Sons strap and has been fully serviced by our watchmaker. We believe this is a steal at this price—just look at what you're getting in this range. Let's get a great deal done! title: Cartier Santos Dumont Black Lacquered ref. WSSA0046 Box and Paper Set
description: The Cartier Santos holds a truly special place in watchmaking history. At the beginning of the 20th century, pioneering aviator Alberto Santos-Dumont complained to his close friend Louis Cartier that pocket watches were impractical to use while flying. In response, Louis Cartier designed a watch that could comfortably be worn on the wrist — creating what is widely considered one of the world’s very first purpose-built wristwatches for men. Equally revolutionary was its design. At a time when nearly all watches featured round cases, the Santos stood apart with its distinctive square shape, exposed screws, and clean geometric lines — elements that would later become defining signatures of Cartier watchmaking. Over the decades, the Santos evolved into one of Cartier’s most iconic collections, balancing elegance, innovation, and everyday wearability. Within the modern range, the Santos-Dumont represents the collection’s more refined and classical side, staying closest in spirit to the original early aviation watches through its slim profile, elegant proportions, and understated design language. The Cartier Santos-Dumont presented here features a fully stainless steel case measuring 31.5 mm wide, 43.5 mm lug-to-lug, with a cabochon topped crown . Cartier classifies this as a “Large” model, though by modern standards it remains wonderfully elegant and restrained in size — exactly as a Santos-Dumont should be. What makes this watch so appealing on the wrist is the way Cartier combines compact proportions with remarkable presence and refinement. The slim profile allows the watch to sit beautifully under a cuff, while the iconic square case architecture gives it far more visual impact than the measurements alone might suggest. A particularly striking detail is the layer of glossy black lacquer surrounding the bezel and upper case surfaces. This subtle contrast adds depth, sharpness, and a distinctly Art Deco character to the design, beautifully emphasizing the Santos-Dumont’s clean geometric lines and timeless elegance. The deep black lacquered dial immediately draws the eye through its beautifully sculpted surface, featuring an engraved geometric pattern that creates a subtle three-dimensional effect depending on the light. Applied Roman numerals rise elegantly from the dial, adding both depth and unmistakable Cartier character. Complementing the architecture of the dial are the signature sword-shaped hands, whose sharp lines perfectly echo the refined geometry of the numerals and case design. Encircling the dial is a finely printed railway minute track — a classic Cartier detail. The watch comes on its original Cartier alligator strap, with a steel Cartier esque pin buckle attached. Furthermore this watch comes with its original inner and outer boxes , the original invoice and the Cartier guarantee card stating sale in sept 2023.
