title: Patek Philippe World Time ref 5130R Guilloché Dial in 18k Rose Gold with Box and Papers
description: The story of the Patek Philippe World Time complication begins with Louis Cottier, a Geneva watchmaker who invented the modern world time mechanism in the early 1930s. His system allowed the wearer to read the time in 24 time zones simultaneously, using a central hour and minute hand, a rotating 24-hour ring, and a city ring representing major world cities. Patek Philippe quickly recognized the brilliance of Cottier’s invention and, in 1937, introduced its first world time wristwatch: Ref. 96 HU (“HU” for Heure Universelle ). Over the following decades, Patek Philippe refined the concept with several legendary references. The Ref. 1415 HU of the 1940s and 1950s featured a larger case and improved legibility, while the Ref. 2523 HU of the 1950s is celebrated for its breathtaking cloisonné enamel dials depicting world maps. Today, the Ref. 2523 is considered the holy grail of Patek Philippe World Time watches, with exceptional examples achieving tens of millions at auction. From the 1970s until around 2000, Patek Philippe produced very few World Time watches, until the introduction of Ref. 5110, which marked the beginning of the modern World Time era. This reference remains a favorite here at Bulang & Sons—an icon that perfectly balances technical ingenuity with timeless elegance. Presented here is its successor, Ref. 5130R, with the “R” denoting its 18k rose gold case. Slightly larger than its predecessor at 39.5mm, the watch features a classic Calatrava-style case and a pusher at 10 o’clock that advances the local time by one hour while simultaneously rotating the city and 24-hour rings, all without disturbing the minute hand. A sapphire display case back reveals the Caliber 240/228 HU, powered by a refined 22k gold micro-rotor. The hands are the distinctive knife style, with a sharp minute hand and an expressive bubble hour hand—an elegant nod to historic World Time models. The dial is a true work of art, adorned with a beautifully executed guilloché pattern in tones that harmonize effortlessly with the warmth of the rose gold case. The outer city ring displays 24 cities, each representing a different time zone, allowing the wearer to travel the world at a single glance. The watch is paired with a beautiful Bulang & Sons leather strap and fitted with its original 18k rose gold Patek Philippe folding buckle. It comes complete with inner and outer boxes, booklets, the leather document holder, and the original Certificate of Origin, confirming its sale in 2007. Fully serviced by our watchmaker, this exceptional world timer is ready for many years of faithful service. More than a watch, this is a companion for a life well travelled — quietly marking time across continents, memories, and moments. Get in touch to make it yours ! title: Cartier Tank Louis Rare Jaeger Movement in 18k yellow gold Paris Dial
description: Few manufacturers have shaped the aesthetics of watchmaking as profoundly as Cartier. Long before wristwatches became commonplace, the maison understood that a watch could be more than a mere instrument for telling time—it could be an expression of style, culture, and refinement. This philosophy gave rise to some of the most enduring and influential designs in horological history. Among them, the Tank stands as Cartier's defining creation. Inspired by the silhouette of military tanks viewed from above during the First World War, its distinctive rectangular case and parallel brancards introduced an entirely new approach to wristwatch design. Over a century later, the Tank remains one of the most recognizable and celebrated watches ever produced. What makes the Tank so remarkable is the contrast between its inspiration and its execution. Cartier transformed the powerful, utilitarian forms of military machinery into an object of elegance and restraint. The result was a design whose origins are almost impossible to detect beneath its timeless sophistication. Among the many iterations of the Tank, the Tank Louis Cartier is widely regarded as the purest expression of the concept. Introduced during the 1920s, it refined the original design through softer lines, gently curved brancards, and more graceful proportions. These subtle changes elevated the Tank from an innovative wristwatch into a true icon of elegance, creating the visual template that collectors immediately recognize today. Presented here is a particularly charming example dating from the early 1970s, crafted in 18k yellow gold and powered by a hand-wound movement supplied by Jaeger-LeCoultre, which is very rare. For many collectors, this detail is especially significant. During this period, Cartier relied on some of Switzerland's finest movement manufacturers, and the presence of a Jaeger-LeCoultre calibre adds an additional layer of desirability to an already exceptional watch. Vintage Cartier production during the 1960s & early 1970s was remarkably limited. Operating primarily through its independent boutiques in Paris, London, and New York, the maison produced watches in relatively small numbers, often with a highly artisanal approach. As a result, surviving examples from this era are considerably rarer than many collectors realize.. Cartier has never published comprehensive production records for this period. However, it is widely understood that watch production during the 1960s and early 1970's remained highly limited, experts estimate that they produced fewer than 100 to a few hundred Tank watches per year in the 1960s. The 30 x 23mm 18k yellow-gold case remains in lovely condition and is further distinguished by a beautifully hand-engraved caseback bearing the touching inscription: "To Rodney... with each passing hour greater love and affection... Billie, December 25, 1973." These personal engravings offer a glimpse into the lives of previous owners and add a romantic layer of prove

title: Rolex Explorer 5504 “Super precision” Gilt Chapter-ring Dial
description: The Explorer has long represented what many consider the perfect “one good watch” to own. Its clean design and understated versatility make it equally suited to everyday life and adventurous escapes. The reference 1016, in particular, holds a special place in watch history—produced for an impressive 29 years, from 1960 to 1989. With its modest 36mm case, no-date dial, and sharp black face—whether gilt or matte—it remains the quintessential vintage Rolex sports watch. Quietly iconic, the Explorer is the Rolex for those who appreciate substance over status. For many watch enthusiasts, including us at Bulang and Sons, a gilt dial Explorer with a chapter ring is the ultimate grail—and when people picture that, they usually think of the Rolex 1016. While this is not a reference 1016, it is the ref. 5504—often overlooked and perhaps even “a forgotten Explorer reference.” Unlike its “brother” reference 5500, which is 34mm, the 5504 retains the full 36mm case size. Let’s break down why this watch is such an interesting one: The 5504 is often mistaken for a 1016, and truth be told, the only real difference is that the 5504 was never chronometer-certified. At the time, this was Rolex’s way of offering a nearly identical model at a lower price point. (Or—depending on how you look at it—charging more for the 1016! 😉) When the 5504 Explorer was first produced in 1958, the chronometer-certified Explorer was actually the Rolex 6610, which used the older caliber 1030 movement that Rolex was beginning to phase out of its sports models. The 5504 was one of the first to feature the newer caliber 1530, which was also used in early Submariners of the time, including the legendary 5508 and 5510 “Big Crown” models—better known as the “James Bond” watches. This newer caliber was compact and highly precise, but it was built as more of a workhorse movement. That’s why it appeared in several non-chronometer models, including early Submariners, the later 5513, and the Air-King. This fine example features a beautiful gilt dial with a chapter ring, bold lume-filled numerals, and silver printing for "Explorer" and "Super Precision." The hands were replaced during a later service and are tritium—no longer glowing under UV light. The riveted Oyster bracelet (ref. 7206) has end links marked 80 and a clasp stamped 2/69. The watch has been fully checked and regulated by our watchmaker and is ready to “explore some more” in the years ahead! It wears beautifully on the wrist—classic and under-the-radar, never loud. Get in touch if this low-key legend speaks to you. description: There is something quietly reassuring about the design language of the Patek Philippe Calatrava—a sense of balance and refinement that has remained largely untouched since the days of the original reference 96. The reference 5026 carries that same spirit, yet with a subtle evolution. It builds upon everything we have come to appreciate about the Calatrava: clean lines, elegant proportions, and a dial that feels both timeless and effortless. At the same time, it introduces a gentle nod to another great name in watchmaking. The interplay between Patek Philippe’s restrained design and the influence of Breguet creates something truly special—an aesthetic that feels familiar, yet just a little different. This particular example, however, tells an even more interesting story. Created as a Millennium edition in the year 2000 and limited to just 130 pieces, it steps slightly away from the expected. Instead of the more commonly seen Arabic numerals, the dial features painted Roman numerals at the quarter hours, balanced by simple stick indices for the remaining markers. It’s a subtle variation, but one that gives the watch its own quiet identity. Inside, the beautifully refined cal. 240 micro-rotor movement—first introduced in 1977—keeps things slim and elegant. The off-centre seconds subdial adds a touch of asymmetry, while the modest 33.5 mm case ensures it wears exactly as a classic Calatrava should: understated and close to the wrist. Produced between 1997 and 2002, the reference 5026 remains one of those pieces that doesn’t seek attention, but rewards those who take the time to look a little closer.
